cards.headline: White took the ko first and also has a free local threat, while Black has none, so Black needs two more threats elsewhere than White: S[KO-2], not S[KO-].

diagrams.caption: The tree's line. White 4 captures the stone at G18 and takes the ko. The tree marks the leaf S[KO-]; the solver said KO−2.

diagrams.moves: G18! C19 D18 F18 G18! pass F18
diagrams.caption: Black 5 retakes after a threat elsewhere. White 6 is a local threat: Black 7 must capture two stones, and White 8 retakes without a threat elsewhere. Black 9 retakes after a second threat elsewhere. White has no local threat left; White 10 plays elsewhere and Black 11 connects: eyes at E19 and on the left, alive.
If Black 7 connects the ko instead of capturing, White 8 captures two stones and Black has only the eye at E19: dead.
Black has no local threat. Black 5 threatens to capture the white stone at A18, but the eye there would be false because B17 is White, so White 6 simply connects the ko: dead.

text: The tree's S[KO-] records only that White 4 took the ko first. But White also has a free local threat. When Black 5 retakes in Diagram 2, White 6 puts the black stones at B18 and B19 in atari, and Black 7 must capture; connecting the ko instead loses those stones and Black dies (Diagram 3). So White 8 retakes without spending a threat elsewhere. White can make the same threat at A19 or D18 instead, but each settles the left side, so White gets only one.

Black has no local threat to match it, at the leaf (Diagram 4) or after White 8 in Diagram 2. So Black needs a second threat elsewhere for Black 9: in all, two more threats elsewhere than White. That is S[KO-2], not S[KO-]. The site's tutorial says local ko threats are usually counted in the S[] label.

Both reviewers agree. Two caveats. Two cases in the solver's ko tables stayed undecided; the decided ones agree, but the verdict rests on move-by-move checks. And the tutorial describes KO−2 as a step ko, while this ko is direct, and its only local-threat example is one that helps the player; counting threats both ways, as besogo does, still gives KO−2.
